utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take your chair. Ms. Korner, appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Barbara Baruch, and Mr. Vujic is lost and I don't know if he is -- has ever been in this courtroom or could figure out how to come in. I apologise for that but he will be joining me today and the reason that he didn't walk in with me is the brand new copier for the Defence was broken and he had to copy a document for the second witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Good morning to you. Madam Registrar, I'm sorry to bother you with this but I need to be able to look at the Defence bench, so if you could perhaps move -- I thank you. They have to be somewhere so... But if -- are they right in front of someone's face over there or not? Because I can't see from here. No? All right. So let's start. We have first the cross-examination of the first witness. Is it closed session or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, it's Ms. Sutherland's witness. I don't know whether you want me to deal with some matters. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I forgot to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all is the timing this week. As a result of - I think - the memo that you've had from VWS as well about the witness who is also due to return for cross-examination on this Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour will have seen the medical certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I haven't, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was attached to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. That hasn't been brought to my attention. Have you seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know nothing about it, actually, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I hand up -- we will get copies arranged but this was given to us by VWS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we propose to do, at the moment, is obviously he can't come back this Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's due -- without at the moment completely -- Your Honour we will arrange for copies, or maybe the usher could arrange for copies for -- no, usher, no, no, no, sorry. It gives the address and the place where the witness resides. We will arrange a copy of the actual certificate but to take out the address but if Your Honours want a copy now the usher could you all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness is medically unfit to travel to The Hague again to give evidence this week. It doesn't say this week. It says medically unfit to travel back and give evidence. Whether that will be possible or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would hope that given he's due to go on a summer holiday and we would hope that given time to get over this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe he would feel better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That he would be feel better and we would ask Your Honour to put it over, perhaps, to go with the experts at the beginning of the Defence case in the hopes that we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, I don't even need to consult my colleagues on this. I can tell you yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that then leaves a gap for Friday for this reason, in that he was originally due to come back for further cross-examination. In addition to that, we had understood from what the Defence had said about the intercept evidence that they wanted the two Rule 92 witnesses brought for cross-examination. We understand that was an error. They don't require them. They want a completely different witness who we are not prepared to put in. If they want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I took it, actually; I kept my mouth shut but it seemed to me there was this misunderstanding. They wanted to cross-examine a witness that you did not mean to bring forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a result of that, there are no witnesses regrettably lined up for Friday because the next witness is not arriving here until the Friday -- I'm sorry, the one that was due on the Monday is only now booked to come in on the Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Accordingly, Your Honour, can I put it this way? I know that on Thursday, there was a discussion as to whether if necessary you would sit and not attend the whole plenary, there will be no necessity for that now. The witness who is coming tomorrow is in any event a major witness and so it's quite -- it will be possible for him to do Tuesday, Wednesday and then the Friday in addition to that, Mr. Koumjian will be ready to deal with legal argument on the admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I was going to suggest actually. That Friday will be used at least in part to discuss or to debate the legality issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Related to the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Koumjian should be prepared for that, okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that applies to Mr. Ackerman as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'll certainly convey that to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, finally, the gentleman who had the car accident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We have been given information that he -- his secretary contacted us on the 10th, Thursday, I think, to say that he -- the tests luckily have proved that he had nothing worse than a broken arm. He was going home on the Friday and then going to Africa on Saturday. If Your Honours are agreeable, would it be possible for him to testify on Thursday the 28th of August, and Friday, the 29th, if need be? Which gives Mr. Ackerman further time as well for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those are just the matters I wish to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is he testifying on two days?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He can -- we had him down for one. If necessary he can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Keep him for one. He's got a written report, no, I suppose. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, he hasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought he was coming over with a written report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's made a statement but there is no written report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, see if we could limit it to one day. It would be better I suppose than two days, what days would those be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thursday the 28th and if necessary, Friday, the 29th. I agree, I hope we could finish him within the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do I understand this correctly, then, that witness plus Friday's witness, plus two cross-examinations that hadn't been done I think of experts all have to be -- the wrap-up in August? No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I gave Mr. Ackerman the choice to -- the idea was to have the cross-examination of the two expert witnesses before Mr. Ackerman starts the Defence case, so we are talking of October -- 6th October is when supposedly the Defence case would start. So the idea was the first two days or three days or - I don't know - would be dedicated to the cross-examination of the expert witnesses. I gave Mr. Ackerman the choice if he prefers to finish those in the last week of August, when we'll be here anyway, he can do that. But it's up to him. I mean, he only needs to liaise with Ms. Korner so that these individuals are present here in The Hague. That's number 1. The gentleman who had the car accident in (Redacted) or wherever he had it - will be coming over 28th, 29th of August, right? And he will be cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman on that occasion. Whether it will be one day or two days, I don't know. It's up to -- more or less up to you. Maybe we need to redact --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, because I -- I have got that benefit of following --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland as you know is very careful about these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, redact, please, Ms. Chuqing, all right? And then there is this guy we are talking about. We don't know actually whether he will be in a position to come over again. However, the suggestion of Ms. Korner, if I read her well, is that he will come forward if at all in October and not the end of August. So that will give him enough time to recover.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood you any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last matter -- I'm sorry, I didn't have a note of that, is the question of -- can I just go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Druzic and welcome back. You know the procedure. Please take the text of the solemn declaration and kindly repeat your undertaking to testify the truth. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Please take a chair. Madam Baruch, I don't know -- you weren't present when he gave evidence, no? He gave evidence, we would have finished with him had things not really happened the way they happened that day and so it's now your turn to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you, may it please the Court. Cross-examined by Ms. Baruch:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Druzic. My name is Barbara Baruch and I represent the defendant in this case. You have not seen me before because the other attorney has not returned to this country. So, I welcome you back and I will ask you some questions, okay? Have you spoken with anybody with regard to your previous testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no need to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you again also haven't spoken with the Prosecutor except for that small matter that the Court permitted to you speak about last time? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's right. This -- this morning I saw the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have a conversation this morning with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that you were an assemblyman back in 1990 from Petrovac out of the SDA party. Are you an assemblyman at the current time?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe that at one point you were president of the board of the commissariat of the Islamic community in Bosanski Petrovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. From 1988 until 1997, the president of the Islamic community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have a position in that community today, aside from -- that's not the Presidency? For example, are you on the board?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am the president of the Dzemat. The Dzemat is composed of methods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is Dzemat is a part of that Islamic community; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's part of the Medzlis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked previously about the population of Bosanski Petrovac, and I think you said you did not know that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the percentage is concerned, those who still live in Bosanski Petrovac, the respective percentages of Muslims, Serbs and Croats, I don't know at the time. But I do know that many Serbs returned to the Bosanski Petrovac area. They returned to their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the present time the majority of the citizens of that municipality are Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Currently, upon their return, I think probably the Serbs are in the majority. Because many people returned to the villages and many of them were Serbs. Tenje Olsik [phoen], Krlici [phoen], Vertoci, Bravsko, Smoljana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony is today you believe once more that the majority of the population is Serb in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Between -- you know, you used the word upon their return. Are you talking about people, Serbs, who have already returned to Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know a person named Isnam Talic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've understood the name, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isnam Talic.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm wondering if you are aware of a movement to change the name of the town from Bosanski Petrovac to something else since 1996?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At that time, I was staying in Germany as a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. refugee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't very clear. Are you aware of a movement to change the name of the town since after the war was over to a Bosnian name as opposed to a name that has Petrovac in it?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Bosanski Petrovac and I'm pushing 50. We did not have Talic as a last name. Isnam Talic that's probably someone's first and last name. As far as my memory goes back, and the memory of my family, Bosanski Petrovac was always there but no Talics were ever present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I switched the subject on you. I should have indicated that to you. Are you aware of anybody involved in a movement to change the name of Bosanski Petrovac to a name that sounds more Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, after I left the camp on the 3rd of November, 1992, until the 9th of April, 1997, I spent this whole period of time in Germany. I am not familiar with any attempts to change the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. My understanding is that before the war, there were four mosques in Bosanski Petrovac, two in town and one in Bijela and one in Rasinovac. I don't know if I said the names correctly but would you agree that before the war those were the number of mosques in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe that before the war, there were 12 Orthodox churches in Bosanski Petrovac. Would you agree, if not with the exact number, approximately that?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of their exact number. I know there were some but I don't know their number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that today there are five mosques in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is only one Orthodox church; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town itself, yes. And it used to be there before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And none others that you know of in the municipality; is that correct? Only one.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell the Defence the following: You probably are not aware of this but the church was there in the village of Krnjavusa and it has been functioning all the time. I believe that they are looking for sponsors to get the churches throughout the remaining villages repaired as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Druzic, my question went to the fact that I believe there were 12 orthodox churches in the town -- in the municipality before the war and now there is only one, regardless of whether it used to be there or did not used to be there. Is that your understanding? Do you only know of one orthodox church now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the town or --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: In the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: In the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the municipality. Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, what's the relevance of this line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the relevance actually. But I don't think you need to answer. I can -- there is a relevance. I mean, how important it is, that's another matter but -- yes, go ahead. Try to answer the question, please. If you know, obviously, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The town, there is one church and it was there before the war. Other churches were in the villages, in the village of Krnjavusa where the largest number of Serb returnees -- which received the largest number of Serb returnees. The church has been put together, redone, and they hold services there, and I'm really surprised that you don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mrs. Baruch doesn't travel to the area. So try to avoid making comments like that, all right? The question was this: It was put to you that where 12 orthodox churches in the municipality before the war and now there is only one. What is your answer? Is it -- is this suggestion correct or not? Or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't go around villages much and in the town, I see the church that I passed by every day and it's active and in the village of Krnjavusa because I had to go to a saw mill there and I could see that the church had been repaired and that it is -- that it can function normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And with regard to any other churches, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't go around villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So, Ms. Baruch, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever at any time fight with the BiH forces in the area of Petrovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I when I was locked up as of the 15th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Druzic, was whether you had -- I'm going to accept your answer as no. Are you aware that about 10 per cent of the Petrovac population fought with the army of the BiH? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The reason I put that to you is because I think you're very much aware of what goes on in the Muslim community in Petrovac and so my question was: Were you aware that 10 per cent of the Muslim community had been fighting with the army of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already answered the question. He's told you no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever -- did the SDA continue to hold meetings after the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person, Kecman, who you heard speak at a rally, was he in your mind the biggest incitement to discord in your area of Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, these questions have already been put by Mr. Cunningham on page 16834.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I know that he talked about Mr. Kecman's speech, but I'm trying to find out if that speech by Kecman and Kecman himself was the biggest incitement to discord in the Petrovac area, municipality, back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What date was that, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 2nd of June, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 6th of June?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 2nd of June. The question was in relation to the remarks made by Mr. Kecman in addition to it being an insult. "Did you see it as a threat to you as a Bosniak" and then the witness answered --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Let me explain, Your Honours. That is not the subject of my question. My question is whether with Kecman, who was from that general area, was the biggest incitement to discord in the area of Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have -- I don't have the 2nd of June transcript here. It must have been in another courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were incarcerated would you agree that Mr. Kecman was the biggest inciter of discord in the Petrovac area?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Other things had begun to happen. What Kecman said, he said at a party promotion, when there were visitors from Belgrade and Stara Basala [phoen]. But in 1992, it was already on its way and I was detained on the 15th of June, 1992, and many things happened before that date, before the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about radio stations during your prior testimony. Could you receive any radio broadcasts from outside of the territory of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bosnia-Herzegovina, outside of the Petrovac area?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't follow television and radio much. Well, I listened to the radio more. There was more switched on to radio Petrovac when they raised the word Bosanski and Milan Latinovic was the editor of the programme. He used to teach at my elementary school and he started the ethnic hatred against Bosniaks. They started with nationalistic songs and at that time it was really impossible to listen to it because it was clear from that that a major evil lay in store for Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You have told us then about Kecman and Latinovic who you said were inciting people but my question went to radio broadcasts. Were you able to receive -- were the people in Petrovac able to receive radio transmissions from Bihac, for example?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about from parts of Croatia? Were they able to receive it from there?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you that I switched on seldom because I was working and I was moving about a great deal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I'm confused. I thought that you were not working since March of 1992, but again, the reason that I'm asking you these questions, Mr. Druzic, is I'm trying to find out if, like today, I can receive AM broadcasts and FM broadcasts, for example, from England while I'm in Holland and my question to you was whether or not you knew if your population in Petrovac could receive outside radio broadcasts and I think what you just told me is that you never listened; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall tell you clearly. For a while, for a long time, one could watch the television of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then our transmitters were destroyed and all the television and radio were then centred on Banja Luka, and as regards the coverage by the transmitter, all television, one could -- one could watch or listen only to those radio stations which were covered by Banja Luka, because the transmitter that we had was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony to this Court is that because the television transmitter was turned so that only Banja Luka television could be seen, that also affected radio waves like FM and AM radio stations from other countries? Is that your testimony? Or did you just not listen to radio at all?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I keep repeating, I didn't listen to the radio much and I didn't really watch television much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you, after you left the former Yugoslavia, did you give money or information regarding the situation in Petrovac to anyone who you considered friendly to or connected to the Bosnian armed forces or the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand what you mean, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't blame him. I suppose you better divide it, separate the two issues because mixing giving money or information is a little bit confusing for the witness, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of the refugees I think were active in collecting money to support Bosnian causes once they left the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Were you involved in that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, maybe -- involved in collecting money or involved as a contributor?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Involved in collecting money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Were you collecting money from amongst Bosniaks to hand over to the Bosnian armed forces or the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, naturally, when I came out, the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina flared up and naturally Muslims and Bosniaks were in closed areas where they could not receive anything, so quite naturally, not only in the place where I was in Germany but the world over, there were clubs which organised raising of funds, of aid for people who were in Bosnia-Herzegovina under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That answers your question. Do you want to put a further question on information or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to information that you may have known about the place you grew up, Bosanski Petrovac, did you also convey information about that area to Bosnian forces, once you left the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, say, my family was in Bihac by and large, and between 1992 and 1995, as you -- you know what kind of communications were with Bihac, nothing could be done, so what contacts are we talking about? But nevertheless, somehow one managed to send something, to one's kin or some people living in those areas, something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about information that would be assisting the BiH forces. Were you able to convey such information about Petrovac to people who could use such information for tactical reasons?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of information could I give them, since I wasn't with the BH Army, since in 1993 I was directly transferred by the UNHCR to Switzerland and then on to Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. I have not disputed that. We all understand that. And the question goes to you having grown up in Bosanski Petrovac were very familiar with the layout of the area, perhaps where reservists in the past had trained, with the structure of the government, where the municipal building was. Did you ever convey information like that, not just that information but information like that, to people whom you knew could use it for a tactical advantage in the ongoing war?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, in wartime, my Petrovac friends were already in Bihac and in Travnik to which they fled on the 24th of September, 1992 so there were already people who had joined the BH army and I don't know why would I have to convey anything to them when my Petrovac friends were already incorporated in the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to take that as your answer under oath, was no, you didn't do that. Would you agree with that? No, you didn't convey information.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, of course. There was no need for it. People were already in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I saw -- you know there are a lot of newspaper articles and Internet articles about the war and I saw something that suggested that people from Bihac liberated Petrovac along with some 20 Bosniaks from Petrovac who fought in the 3rd and 7th corps and especially in the 3rd and 17th Brigades. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know this is Ms. Sutherland's witness but really, Your Honour, we have a fairly tight schedule. What is the relevance of the events of 1995 to what happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the relevance, Ms. Baruch?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1995, Your Honour and if he was going to tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you're talking about the liberation of Bosanski Petrovac and that did not occur before 1995, for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Druzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: The basis, I indicated, was an internet article that I saw that had the date 1992, Your Honour so I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This witness is here again because Mr. Cunningham had about five minutes, if I remember well, or ten minutes, left for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unfortunately things went haywire that day and so and we have the next witness in line.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm not going to interfere with that, Your Honour. I am finished with my questions to this witness. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thanks. So Mr. Druzic, thanks for being patient with us and being cooperative, for having come again. I know this was unfortunate, indeed, that you had to come back. Things went wrong last time, as you know, and we needed you to come back, we couldn't finish with you on that occasion. So once more I thank you on behalf of everyone and I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you. Madam usher will escort you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next witness is also without any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and he will be giving evidence in English. He speaks perfect English. I've told him that if he has any problems with the -- any words then of course he can say it in the Bosnian language and then it will be interpreted but for the majority, I think it will be in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That makes things easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand, you said yes he is, Ms. Korner -- you mean -- yes, he is not protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's not a protected witness, no. I understood Mr. Ackerman was going to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: If this witness is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, it's me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 7.89. When is Mr. Cunningham coming back, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Tuesday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tuesday, that's tomorrow, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe Mr. Ackerman is taking the witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure there is nothing wrong with either of them. Basically it's all right. Who is leading this witness, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, bring him in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pasic. Welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, our Rules require that you enter a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper that Madam usher is handing to you. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a chair. I understand you have opted to testify in the English language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which makes things easier for everyone. If at any time you get stuck with any word and you've got difficulties, you can go back to your own language. There are interpreters following what you're saying in any case, so any word that you may use from your own language will be immediately interpreted into English and into French so you don't need to bother about that. Ms. Korner will ask you a series of questions put a series of questions to you first and then she will be followed by Madam Baruch who is appearing for Mr. Brdjanin, who is the accused in this case. Ms. Korner. Examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, is your name Elvedin Pasic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One thing I forgot to warn you about yesterday is because we are both going to be speaking English, it's important that there is a pause between you answering my question and when you've answered it, me asking the next so the interpreters can catch up. And you'll find that I'm the worst offender in that respect. Mr. Pasic, were you born on the 3rd of June, 1978, in Hrvacani, in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time we are going to deal with the events of between June and November of 1992, you would have been 13, just 14; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you first of all, please, to look at a map of Kotor Varos, which is Exhibit P2120. Just put that on the ELMO. Usher, you're going to have to put it slightly -- can we go? Yes. Can you just -- I think we can all see it but we see Kotor Varos and is Hrvacani to the right of Kotor Varos town as we look at it, the intervening village being shown as Cirkino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And roughly how far?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are sorry but the interpreters cannot hear the witness at all. Could the witness speak up, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher we need to put -- either bring the witness forward or move the microphones nearer to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I see Hrvacani on the right of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far roughly, in terms of distance was it from the centre of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'd say 13 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your village, roughly how many houses were there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: 100 houses, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And although it's not marked, I don't think, on the map, was there a village called Tepici very close to your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Hrvacani, as we can see on the map, a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it follow, therefore, and I should have asked you that earlier, that you yourself were a Muslim by nationality -- are a Muslim by nationality?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what about Tepici? What was the nationality of the inhabitants of that village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then was there another village called Savici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that located, in terms of your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: East side of Hrvacani, which is on the map -- should be on the right side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the nationality of those inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Those were all 100 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had a Serb village to the east, and Tepici was where in relation to --

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: North.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And were they the same size as your village or smaller or bigger?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Tepici was much smaller and Savici, not as big as Hrvacani but bigger than Tepici so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's all I think we need look at for the moment at the map save we may as well just for a moment identify two other places that we are going to hear about, three. First of all, Dabovci. Was that a village that you were familiar with or became familiar with?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any relatives living in that village? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had. I had my sister, who was married to her husband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And we can see then also Vrbanjci and then Vecici done below your --

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, yes, you can put the map away now. Now, the school that you attended, where was that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: It was located five kilometres from Hrvacani and in Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a mixed school, in other words Serbs, Muslims and were there any Croats there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am. It was mixed: Serbs, Muslims and Croats together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have friends in all ethnicities, all nationalities?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think as far as your family was concerned, before the war began, was your father working in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But visited you on weekends?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have an older brother, Ahmedin.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the sister who you described was married and living in Dabovci. Was that Hamida?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those days, what was her married name?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Hamida -- I don't remember the last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, don't worry. If we can just jump ahead I think it's right that you're going to describe to us her husband was killed and she has since remarried; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you notice a change taking place in the general situation in your area around May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe what first struck you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Sure. When I was attending the 7th grade, almost at the end of the school year, we noticed on several army movements which was taking place from -- army coming from Kotor Varos, moving towards Doboj and they were definitely JNA members. I remember one day I was standing waiting for our bus and the convoy was approximately 30 vehicles and the soldiers there were waving at us, point 3, the symbol, and we -- that was the first time we noticed a large movement, and we asked our teachers and friends what's going on, and they told us not to worry about it because it's just an activity and exercise from side of JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, those you could tell were JNA members. How were you able to say that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Because they were specially vehicles, they were marked by JNA and also the soldiers were wearing regular olive-green, whatever, uniforms, marked JNA. Some of them were camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. What about your neighbouring Serbs? Did you notice anything about them and the way they were dressing?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. We know -- first time I noticed it, drastic changes and behaviour, our neighbours, was the second day of our holiday called Bajram when we noticed our neighbouring Serbs from Tepici and Savici were digging trenches, and some of them from Novakovo Brdo -- we noticed two tanks were pointing at our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get on to what happened on the Bajram holiday, before you noticed that they were digging trenches and you saw these tanks, you described the JNA convoy. Was anybody outside the JNA wearing uniforms? The official JNA, I should say.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, ma'am. All I know is just they were JNA uniforms and also some camouflage uniforms too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's move to the Baj -- second day of the Bajram holiday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there is going to be any dispute about that, we intend to put in a document on the religious holidays but we've heard evidence it was June 11 was the first day of the Bajram holiday but we are proposing to put a document in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the second day of that holiday you say you noticed that trenches were being dug by the Serbs in Tepici and Savici and that you noticed two tanks. Where did you see the tanks?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: They were located above Dabovci which Novakovo Brdo faced south from Hrvacani -- faced Hrvacani and I could see clearly because part of my house -- my house was located south -- southwest of Hrvacani it was a straight to the -- faced to the Novakovo Brdo and it was clearly and easy to see Novakovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of seeing these things did anybody from your village go to investigate?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Two well-known and rich -- richest people in Hrvacani called Muho and Murat Dugonjic. After seeing all this movement they wanted to talk to your neighbours in Savici and Tepici and they talked to him in my middle school which was located in between Tepici and Savici. So they asked them, you know, what is all this movement and what is all this digging trenches going -- why is this going on? And they told us not to worry because we were neighbours, it's just a JNA exercise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any Serbs arrive in your village at all?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what manner?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: One day we were sitting in the middle of our village, which was located underneath of a mosque and that's where all men and women, children, we normally meet, have fun, it was approximately around noon when five armed -- well-armed soldiers approached from our south side. They were just walking with some of them JNA uniforms -- JNA uniforms and camouflage uniforms, wearing automatic weapons. They were just passing by and looking at the houses, and as a matter of fact, they did said they greeted -- they said hello to us when they were approaching us, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any -- did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: One person, Boro Tepic, and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did he come from?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I guess he came from Tepici but normally they came from the direction from Vrbanjci. They were walking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what effect did that have on the people in your village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: The people -- affect because that point we knew that something is going to happen, and this actually meant war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you think that? Or what was it about the visit of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Well, we heard that these five soldiers had a bet with some other soldiers that they going to walk through the Hrvacani and -- with armed weapons and everything, so that, you know, something happens that could cause a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As a result of the tanks that you had seen and the trenches and these soldiers walking through your village, what did the villagers in your village decide to do?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we knew that there was no options but to get prepared for this, because obviously we tried to contact our families, like I wanted to -- I tried to contact my sister, the telephone lines, they were mixed up, later on they were disconnected, and we just prayed to God and we were waiting to see what's going to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present at any kind of meeting where the defence of Hrvacani was discussed?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know about meetings but I'll say that our tradition during the holiday is to -- for our hodza, to walk every house and just to sit and talk to the -- eat lunch, that's our celebration. But second day of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bajram, hodza came to our house and our house was quite a big house. A lot of people came, I'd say, but only men came to the house and they were sitting, you know, that's a tradition and they were discussing, I remember I was in the room when they were discussing what we going to ask -- asking question, what we going to do because we see our neighbours digging trenches and obviously this is going to be -- this is it. And at that moment, they start talking and my father told me to leave the room. Don't know what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were you ever aware of any kind of order, either being issued over the radio or by police officers coming to the village, that the people in your village should surrender their hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your brother Ahmedin, where was he at this period?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: At this period, he was attending military academy at Belgrade, and I believe that night he came actually we got surprised because he came from Belgrade, you know, in all this mess, he came -- he came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can we come, please, to the night of the second day of your holiday, around the 13th of June? Did you hear anything coming from the direction of Tepici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. We heard soldier using megaphones, I don't know what else but we could hear him talking and saying, [Interpretation] "Happy Bajram, balija, we will be there soon. And Muho and Murat brew us a coffee and get some baklava ready for us, traditional cake. We will be there soon."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were using -- saying that through megaphones, were they?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they name anybody from your village in particular?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I just mentioned Muho and Murat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They didn't show up in the transcript but he did mention the two names that we find also in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I suppose these were two very well known persons in the village, and they were quite rich too, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, I suppose, Ms. Korner, I think we better pronounce the names, because they didn't make it. Murat and Muho Dugonjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this use of the megaphone go on for?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I would say 15 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Then bombing and shelling started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the bombing and the shelling started, using the megaphones, did these people give any warning that the village was about to be shelled?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there were any ultimatums given, in other words surrender yourselves or the village will be shelled?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there women and children, like yourself and younger, in the village at the time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just ask you this: Did the holiday mean that families tried to get together for that holiday?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so had the -- did people come back to the village who might otherwise not have been there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what happened when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I was in a house located to my left, my cousin, we were down in the basement when the shelling and bombing started. I don't know at that moment where my father was and my brother, but I know for a fact that he came early -- that whole night was horrible, bombing and shelling going on, but early in the morning he came back and he knocked at the window and told us to leave, because neighbouring houses they were burning from shelling and that we were the only ones left in the -- actually in the village of Hrvacani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So by the time he came to find you, he was telling you that everybody else had left?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you and your brother and your mother then leave or your cousin? I'm sorry, you said, I think, your cousin.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you left, was the village deserted?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'd say 98 per cent. Some people left, old people like Ahmedin left in the Hrvacani and I know for a fact that Ibro Dugonjic who was a religious man, he certainly stayed there in the Hrvacani because he didn't want to leave his house, but, yeah, 98 per cent of people left for Plitska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Plitska was how close?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'd say one to two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what nationality were the inhabitants of Plitska?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you left your village, was the shelling still going on?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any kind of shooting going on?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Okay. When we were about to leave our -- we were down in a low -- in between two regions, between Plitska and Hrvacani, when we were trying to cross one open area and we had snipers shooting from Novakovo Brdo and Tepici at us, and we had to crawl up on the hill in open space where we got shot from Novakovo Brdo and Tepici by the snipers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Once you'd got away from your village, what happened to the men? For example your father and your brother?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: My brother and my father, we met them halfway distance to Plitska. They were running like with the children and civilians, but when we got to Plitska, they disappeared. As a matter of fact, I think they went with -- all the men gathered together and they went somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that stage, did you know where they were going?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've told us that some people stayed behind in Hrvacani, including a Mr. Ismet Dugonjic, who was an elderly man and religious. Did you discover later what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. They all got killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you discover this?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'd say 30 days later, when we decided, when we were going back and forth from Bilice and Plitska to Garici, back and forth, we decided to move back to our village, even though it was destroyed, we decided to just go there and live there and at that moment we found the bodies and we found the body of Ibro Dugonjic in his house. He was burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That was jumping ahead slightly. Now, you went first of all to Plitska and from there, did you go to Bilice?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that all of you from Hrvacani or just some of you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Some of us went to Bilice and some of us went to Cirkino Brdo with the relatives, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you go first of all to Cirkino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had that been attacked at all?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, because they signed a loyalty to Serbs and they surrendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, how long did you stay in Cirkino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'd say approximately 20 to 30 days, I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was there? Was it you and your mother?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, and my -- my cousin and most of my relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What made you leave Cirkino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Not enough food and 15 of -- families were living in the house of -- on Cirkino Brdo and not enough food and water so we decided just to go to Plitska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did the authorities raise any problem about you staying in Cirkino Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Hasan Vilic was a man who gave us his old house to live in and Serbs who were in charge, they were in Vrbanjci at that time, they found out that Cirkino Brdo had some civilians from Hrvacani and they told Hasan Vilic, to let us go. If they come back and find civilians from Hrvacani they will kill him and every one of us so at that moment he came to us and told us the whole story and we didn't want to cause any trouble so we left for Bilice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Bilice, was that also a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What preparations had the villagers there made against attack?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'd say they were well organised. They had -- as a matter of fact, when we were coming to Bilice, we met 20 to 30 well-armed men, who were mainly Croats. They had camouflage uniforms and they were well-organised. They were prepared for war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had they taken any precautions to prevent people reaching the village, Serbs reaching the village? In other words, were there trenches?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, there were trenches. As -- when we were approaching the north side of Bilice, we were stopped by soldiers, they were digged -- they had trenches in front of the houses and they knew that we were coming because somebody informed them so they came out and they offered us food and water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people in your -- were there in your group that went from Cirkino Brdo to Bilice?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Twenty to thirty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you got there, did you find that your father was there and your brother?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: When we got to Bilice later on we found out we were in the house who -- of -- who gave -- a Croat family gave us a house and that night, I remember it was raining. My brother and my father, all of them, mainly all men from Hrvacani were there at Plitska at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to your father and the other men from Hrvacani? Did they stay in Bilice or did they go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Some of them stayed in Bilice and some of them left for Vecici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the purpose of them leaving for Vecici was what?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: To defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm moving on to the next part of the travel so perhaps that would be a convenient moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm so sorry, I think it was my fault that you were waiting. I lost time of when we were coming back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Ms. Korner is going to proceed with the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Pasic, we had reached the part where you were in Bilice. Was there sufficient food for all of you from Hrvacani to reside there for any length of time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But I know one thing we were sharing the food with them -- villagers from Bilice and they were sharing food with us. It was somehow organised as we were getting the food once in the morning, you know, they were just giving us, offering us flour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In any event, as you've already, I think, mentioned, did you make a decision to go back to Hrvacani?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By that stage, who was left from the village? Were there any military-aged men left?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: From -- can you repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your village, yes.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: From Hrvacani? Well, most of them, like I mentioned before, they left, some of them left for Vecici and some stayed in Bilice but civilians -- like I said the food was running low, and we decided just to go back and go back to our village and just live there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so who went back?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Just the civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By that, who do you mean, women, children?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Women and children mainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember roughly how many of you there were?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I'll say 30 to 50 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you go back to your village through Plitska where you'd been before?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you were going towards Hrvacani, did you see any Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. We were stopped by two soldiers near my village, walking by, and they were armed with camouflage uniforms. One of them I assume he was -- maybe injured or wounded, I don't know, but he was holding his stomach like this and he was down, he was in big pain, and they stopped us and asked us where -- where are you balija going? And at that moment, my mom and some other old lady stood in front of the group and said we are going back to our village because we have no where to go. And at that moment, a soldier said, we don't care if you balija get killed. There is no place for you here. Go back to Turkey. That's where you belong. And we didn't say anything, we just -- and he says, if you guys get killed or get shot, nobody is going to be responsible for you balijas -- so -- and they left, they left towards Novakovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told them where you were going. Did they tell you what sort of state Hrvacani was in?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. They told us that Hrvacani belonged to Serb republic and that it is -- no longer belongs to us. And there is nothing, everything was burned and destroyed there, no place to live. At that moment my mom said, "We are going and we are just going to find something because there is no place anywhere else for us but home."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Hrvacani, what sort of state was it in?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: First of all, we approached Hrvacani from the south side where first house we crossed by was my long time -- belonged to my uncle and it was totally destroyed. The rest of -- I mean, the rest of the houses burned, just the walls and two chimneys still up but everything else was burned and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said earlier on there were 100 houses roughly in Hrvacani.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many of them were still --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll say, Your Honour, approximately 2 to 5 houses because they were just under constructions and nothing in them, just two naked houses standing, but I'd say two to five houses in the whole village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The rest were more or less in one way or another destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Destroyed by shelling or by people setting fire to them?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Some of them they were -- were destroyed by shelling and most of them burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had happened to the property inside the houses?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: The property in most houses is just gone because when we visit our house, when we approached our house, nothing, no furniture, nothing, was in there, just the walls and I found some things like a Koran, which is a book for Muslims to pray. That was left on the floor. It was burned but some script was left and I got it from -- but everything else was taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you own a dog?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what had happened to the dog?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: We owned -- my father owned a dog because he was a hunter, and he used the dog to hunt animals. When we approached the home and we found him dead. He was shot and dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the villagers own cattle?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. We owned -- my house owned four cattles, and when we were in Plitska and Cirkino Brdo, we saw Serbs, they were taking all the cattles, gathering them together and they were transporting them to Tepici and Savici by tractors and trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a mosque in Hrvacani?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, in the middle of village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what had happened to that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Mosque was completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see, by looking at it, whether that destruction had happened through shelling or through any other kind of attack?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: First, when we came to village, we met in the middle of village where, you know, most of the time we hang out before the war, and we wanted to visit the mosque and clearly, we went over there, mosque was destroyed by -- it was blown up, not because of shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the walls of the houses, what -- has anything been written?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. We found JNA and sayings, this is Serbia, and also marks, a cross with four S's, for C's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you've already told us, was it at that stage that you discovered the bodies of the people who had remained behind?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, having seen the state of the village, what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Well, we decided, we met in the middle of village and some people decided to stay because they found some food and they decided to stay, but my mom and I, we had a family members in Garici, which was signed a loyalty and surrendered to the Serbs so we decided to go to Garici. We didn't want to stay because everything was destroyed and we didn't have food, so we decided to go to Garici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were still in Hrvacani, did some soldiers arrive?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, like 15 to 30 minutes after we arrived at Hrvacani, a full tractor of soldiers was coming from Tepici down to meet us in the centre of village. Some of them they were masked and some of them they had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you recognise any of these people?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: I didn't but my mom did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these soldiers speak to you all?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. As a matter of fact they offered us, one guy offered us water, and ten minutes later they got us water but -- and they told us, why we are here? There is no place for us to stay. And some of us approached and told we want to go to Garici. We don't want to stay but some group, I'd say half the group stayed in Hrvacani, so half the soldiers went with us for Garici and the other half stayed with the group in Hrvacani and I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said one of them gave you water. Was the attitude of all these soldiers friendly towards you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. He was very friendly. He was as a matter of fact helping one pregnant woman, and he got us water. He was really, really friendly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the rest of the soldiers? Were they as friendly?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they doing? Or what was one of them doing?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: One of them, you know, he -- as I mentioned before, he went crazy and he says, there is no place for us, why we are coming back? This is Serbia and if we decided to stay in Hrvacani, they are not going to guarantee for our lives so if we get killed, I mean they would just threaten us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you and your mother went to Garici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that together with most of the people?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to go to Garici, did you have to pass through Savici?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something happen there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
utterances.text: As we were entering Savici, a lot of civilians were waiting for us, and as a matter of fact, I remember Dalibor, name of a guy who was going to school with me, his mom was really crazy, I'll say crazy because she was yelling at us and she wanted, as a matter of fact, to shoot at us because she was going to grab a gun from a soldier who was holding us and she was really, really threaten us because she said, you balija are going around here looting and our soldiers getting killed in Vecici. Let me kill one of the balija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was she prevented from doing anything?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC
